subject: Cognitive Science
title: Regret and Anticipated Regret
description: A short lesson to help you apply Regret and Anticipated Regret.

hook.text: You miss a flight by 5 minutes and feel devastated. Miss it by 2 hours and you shrug. Same outcome, different pain.

buildup.text: Regret scales with how close you came to a better outcome. Near-misses sting more than distant ones.

discovery.text: We also feel more regret for actions than inactions—even when doing nothing costs more.

twist.text: Anticipated regret shapes future decisions. People avoid choices that might later make them feel bad.

climax.text: This drives loss aversion: the pain of losing feels twice as strong as the pleasure of winning the same amount.

punchline.text: We decide not just for outcomes—but to avoid future regret.

quiz.question: Why does missing a flight by 5 minutes hurt more than by 2 hours?

details.summary: Regret is the pain of imagining a better outcome from a different choice. Anticipated regret is the fear of that feeling before you decide. Both powerfully shape decisions, often causing people to avoid action because acts of commission generate more regret than acts of omission.
details.whyItMatters: Regret aversion explains inaction bias, reluctance to switch, and preference for the status quo. People optimize not just for outcomes but for minimizing future regret.
takeaways: Regret from action feels stronger than regret from inaction
Anticipated regret makes people avoid risky choices
Regret aversion reinforces the status quo bias

faq.question: Why does action produce more regret than inaction?
faq.answer: When you act and something goes wrong, you can clearly imagine the counterfactual of not acting. Inaction feels less responsible because you did not cause anything; things just happened. However, in the long term, people regret inaction more, missed opportunities, than failed attempts.

faq.question: How does anticipated regret influence decisions?
faq.answer: People mentally simulate what they would feel if each option turned out badly. Options with higher anticipated regret are avoided even if their expected value is higher. This is why people stick with familiar brands, stay in unsatisfying jobs, and avoid investments with upside risk.
